1.pericope_label: Concerning the Ammonites, thus saith the Lord; Hath Israel no sons? hath he no heir? why then doth their king inherit Gad, and his people dwell in his cities? Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will cause an alarm of war to be heard in Rabbah of the Ammonites; and it shall be a desolate heap, and her daughters shall be burned with fire: then shall Israel be heir unto them that were his heirs, saith the Lord. Howl, O Heshbon, for Ai is spoiled: cry, ye daughters of Rabbah, gird you with sackcloth; lament, and run to and fro by the hedges; for their king shall go into captivity, and his priests and his princes together.

schools.summary: Sketch the long rivalry over the trans-Jordan territory and settle the disputed place-names, holding Heshbon Ammonite and inferring a second Ai beyond the river.
Trace the descent from Lot, date the sentence to a time of Ammonite security so that the faithful must learn to wait, and defend the prophets' figurative style.
Date the whole collection to the siege of Tyre and read the inheritance clause by the ordinary law of succession.
Casts the opening verse as a lawsuit over an illegal encroachment, with a writ of enquiry into Ammon's title.

positions.position: A city of Moab on the Ammonite border; some make it a double city divided by a river, one side to each people.
Strictly an Ammonite city, despite its earlier appearance among the fortunes of Moab.
The summons implies the former royal residence was then in Ammonite hands.

outliers.claim: Presses the legal figure to its worst count, that there were heirs of Israel's own body yet unborn whom the Ammonites barbarously murdered to forestall the claim.
Offers the walls by which the dead were commonly buried as the sense of the hedges, or else the villages called the daughters of the capital, against Ellicott's sheepfolds and vineyard walls.

themes: Concerning the Ammonites, thus saith the Lord; Hath Israel no sons? hath he no heir? why then doth their king inherit Gad, and his people dwell in his cities?

Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will cause an alarm of war to be heard in Rabbah of the Ammonites; and it shall be a desolate heap, and her daughters shall be burned with fire: then shall Israel be heir unto them that were his heirs, saith the Lord.

Howl, O Heshbon, for Ai is spoiled: cry, ye daughters of Rabbah, gird you with sackcloth; lament, and run to and fro by the hedges; for their king shall go into captivity, and his priests and his princes together.

4.pericope_label: Wherefore gloriest thou in the valleys, thy flowing valley, O backsliding daughter? that trusted in her treasures, saying, Who shall come unto me? Behold, I will bring a fear upon thee, saith the Lord God of hosts, from all those that be about thee; and ye shall be driven out every man right forth; and none shall gather up him that wandereth. And afterward I will bring again the captivity of the children of Ammon, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Describe the country as a plateau cut by streams, offer two renderings of the flowing valley, and note that the epithet given to Ammon had been used of the northern kingdom.
Take the valleys for fortified places rather than fertile ones, and read the closing promise as a prelude of the calling of the Gentiles.
Warn against glorying in fruitfulness or power, and look for a historical return under the edict of Cyrus or a conversion to Christ.

debates.question: What are the valleys Ammon gloried in?

positions.position: Fertile well-watered vales producing large crops, in which the whole country lay.
Fortified places: ringed by mountains, they thought themselves unapproachable.
Fruitful ground indeed, but not to be gloried in, since a stronger is coming.
A historical return, on the permission given by the edict of Cyrus.
The conversion of the Ammonites with other heathen to Christ, a prelude of the calling of the Gentiles.

outliers.claim: Explains the delay itself: the prediction was uttered while Ammon was secure and years passed before it took effect, the faithful being held in suspense so as to learn to wait for the fixed time.

Finds it suggestive that the epithet given to Ammon here is the one the same prophet had applied to the northern kingdom, and supposes Ammon too had known the opportunity of worshipping the God of Israel.

themes: Wherefore gloriest thou in the valleys, thy flowing valley, O backsliding daughter? that trusted in her treasures, saying, Who shall come unto me?
Behold, I will bring a fear upon thee, saith the Lord God of hosts, from all those that be about thee; and ye shall be driven out every man right forth; and none shall gather up him that wandereth.
And afterward I will bring again the captivity of the children of Ammon, saith the Lord.

7.pericope_label: Concerning Edom, thus saith the Lord of hosts; Is wisdom no more in Teman? is counsel perished from the prudent? is their wisdom vanished? Flee ye, turn back, dwell deep, O inhabitants of Dedan; for I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time that I will visit him. If grapegatherers come to thee, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, they will destroy till they have enough.

schools.summary: Give the political sequence of Edom's subjection and revolts, and treat the passage as a reproduction of the shorter prophecy with the comparison applied directly to the enemy.
Ground the guilt in kinship and circumcision, and make the shorter prophecy the true interpreter from which this one borrows.
Trace the quarrel to Esau's disinheritance, and read the flight through the Arab custom of vanishing into the desert.
Gives the reason for recording the doom at all, that Edom's triumph and joy over Israel's calamity aggravated the affliction, so the sentence stands as comfort as well as warning.

debates.question: How does this oracle stand to the shorter prophecy against Edom?

positions.position: Obadiah came first and is the true interpreter; this prophet has borrowed from him, and where the earlier spoke of a future thing this one exults over a judgment near at hand.
The expressions are borrowed, and the harmony follows from all the prophets being inspired by one and the same Spirit.
A reproduction, but altered: what the earlier prophet offers as a comparison is here applied directly to the enemy, and the parallel does not license importing its interrogative particle.
Speaks of the words as reproduced in Obadiah rather than taken from it.

outliers.claim: Reports and rejects two readings of the oracle, one referring it to a future destruction of Rome and another making the Jews themselves its object, preferring to take it properly and literally of the Idumeans.
Notes a silence he thinks significant, that unlike Moab and Ammon there is nowhere any promise that Edom's captivity should be brought back.

themes: Concerning Edom, thus saith the Lord of hosts; Is wisdom no more in Teman? is counsel perished from the prudent? is their wisdom vanished?
Flee ye, turn back, dwell deep, O inhabitants of Dedan; for I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time that I will visit him.
If grapegatherers come to thee, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, they will destroy till they have enough.

10.pericope_label: But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself: his seed is spoiled, and his brethren, and his neighbours, and he is not. Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive; and let thy widows trust in me. For thus saith the Lord; Behold, they whose judgment was not to drink of the cup have assuredly drunken; and art thou he that shall altogether go unpunished? thou shalt not go unpunished, but thou shalt surely drink of it.

schools.summary: Reads the promise to the fatherless as genuine pity rather than irony, and takes the cup imagery from an earlier chapter as an argument from the greater to the less.
Gloss the hidden things as treasures and press the total stripping, taking the promise to widows as threatening rather than comfort.
Treat widows and orphans as the peculiar care of God, and read the cup as a rule that no Edomite can expect what no Israelite obtained.

debates.question: Is the word to the fatherless and the widows mercy or irony?

positions.position: Threatening: the words are not spoken by way of promise and comfort, and there would be no Edomites left to say them.
Genuine mercy: widows and orphans are the peculiar care of God, and even Esau's shall be cared for by the Lord.
Not stern irony but a mingling of pity for the helpless, which is truer to this prophet's character.

outliers.claim: Uses the total exposure of the hidden treasures to confirm the earlier comparison, that this would be no grape-gathering or common robbery since God meant to empty them of everything they had.

Names the drinkers of the cup outright as the Jews, who in comparison with others did not deserve it and yet drank, and turns it into a rule that where an Israelite has not escaped an Edomite must not expect to.

themes: But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself: his seed is spoiled, and his brethren, and his neighbours, and he is not.
Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive; and let thy widows trust in me.

For thus saith the Lord; Behold, they whose judgment was not to drink of the cup have assuredly drunken; and art thou he that shall altogether go unpunished? thou shalt not go unpunished, but thou shalt surely drink of it.

13.pericope_label: For I have sworn by myself, saith the Lord, that Bozrah shall become a desolation, a reproach, a waste, and a curse; and all the cities thereof shall be perpetual wastes. I have heard a rumour from the Lord, and an ambassador is sent unto the heathen, saying, Gather ye together, and come against her, and rise up to the battle. For, lo, I will make thee small among the heathen, and despised among men. Thy terribleness hath deceived thee, and the pride of thine heart, O thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, that holdest the height of the hill: though thou shouldest make thy nest as high as the eagle, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Locate Bozrah, prefer the fortresses of Sela to the clefts of the rock, and identify the terribleness with an idol of the Priapic type.
Take the rumour for a formal proclamation by God's heralds, and prefer a reading in which God derides a pride that contended against nature.
Treat Bozrah as a part standing for the whole, and reduce the herald to God's stirring up of the nations.

debates.question: What is the ambassador sent among the nations?

positions.position: A formal proclamation published by God's own heralds, the figure drawn from men proclaiming war; the word must not be reduced to a rumour.
The Lord as great King sending out his envoy to summon the nations against Edom.
Only that God gave permission and stirred up the hearts of these nations against a doomed people.
Speech after the manner of earthly princes who send ambassadors, the substance being that God inclined them to come.

outliers.claim: Reports the majority reading, that Edom is made contemptible because God casts it from its dignity, and prefers his own, that God derides a pride which ought to have restrained itself because it contended against nature.
Reports a division over whether being made small describes what Edom was at the first, a people few in number, or what Edom was to become, and takes the latter.

themes: For I have sworn by myself, saith the Lord, that Bozrah shall become a desolation, a reproach, a waste, and a curse; and all the cities thereof shall be perpetual wastes.
I have heard a rumour from the Lord, and an ambassador is sent unto the heathen, saying, Gather ye together, and come against her, and rise up to the battle.
For, lo, I will make thee small among the heathen, and despised among men.

Thy terribleness hath deceived thee, and the pride of thine heart, O thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, that holdest the height of the hill: though thou shouldest make thy nest as high as the eagle, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the Lord.

17.pericope_label: Also Edom shall be a desolation: every one that goeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss at all the plagues thereof. As in the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighbour cities thereof, saith the Lord, no man shall abide there, neither shall a son of man dwell in it. Behold, he shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan against the habitation of the strong: but I will suddenly make him run away from her: and who is a chosen man, that I may appoint over her? for who is like me? and who will appoint me the time? and who is that shepherd that will stand before me?

schools.summary: Documents the long delay of the fulfilment through the Hasmonean and Roman periods, and rebuilds the lion image from the jungle-forests and pasturage of the Jordan.
Explain the repetition as fixing an incredible thing in the heart, and concede a scattered remnant that never again formed one people.
Press the comparison with the overthrown cities and identify the chosen man as Nebuchadnezzar, or else reverse the parts and make Edom the attacker.

debates.question: Who is the lion coming up from the Jordan?

positions.position: A king and his army, namely Nebuchadnezzar, chosen and commissioned by God against Idumea.
The Chaldaean invasion pictured as a lion working through the jungle and rushing on the flocks of a meadow tract.
The Edomites themselves, coming up fiercely against the invader and then fleeing even out of their own country.

outliers.claim: Insists the words received no immediate or even rapid fulfilment, Idumea being populous under John Hyrcanus and Petra rebuilt by the Romans with baths and theatres, before the land disappears from history in the ninth Christian century.
Grants that some remnant of the nation probably survived, and reconciles it with the prophecy by holding that the survivors were so scattered that they never again formed one people.

themes: Also Edom shall be a desolation: every one that goeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss at all the plagues thereof.
As in the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighbour cities thereof, saith the Lord, no man shall abide there, neither shall a son of man dwell in it.

Behold, he shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan against the habitation of the strong: but I will suddenly make him run away from her: and who is a chosen man, that I may appoint over her? for who is like me? and who will appoint me the time? and who is that shepherd that will stand before me?

20.pericope_label: Therefore hear the counsel of the Lord, that he hath taken against Edom; and his purposes, that he hath purposed against the inhabitants of Teman: Surely the least of the flock shall draw them out: surely he shall make their habitations desolate with them. The earth is moved at the noise of their fall, at the cry the noise thereof was heard in the Red sea. Behold, he shall come up and fly as the eagle, and spread his wings over Bozrah: and at that day shall the heart of the mighty men of Edom be as the heart of a woman in her pangs.

schools.summary: Deny that Teman is a synonym for Edom, re-parse the clause about the flock, and note that the passage recurs later applied to Babylon.
Read the fall as a mass whose crash terrifies the neighbours, and point out that the Chaldeans were then Edom's friends.
Treat Teman as a synonym supplied for variety and name the eagle as Nebuchadnezzar.

debates.question: Is Teman simply another name for Edom?

positions.position: Yes: a synonym used to prevent monotony and give variety to the versification.
No: Teman is named separately because its people were particularly famous for the wisdom the oracle opened by mocking.

debates.question: What does the clause about the least of the flock mean?

positions.position: The Edomites are timid sheep, and the weakest foe will overcome them.
The least of the invader's forces will drag them from their hiding places.
The object has been mistaken for the subject: the invaders will vex them, the feeble ones of the flock, and make their pasturage terror-stricken at them.

outliers.claim: Supplies the circumstance that gives the threat its force, that when it was spoken nobody could have suspected the Chaldeans would become enemies of Edom, the two being on the best of terms.

Leaves the noise of the fall open between the shout of the conquerors, the cry of the Edomites and the report of the disaster, and suspects an allusion to the falling of the rocks in which that country abounded.

themes: Therefore hear the counsel of the Lord, that he hath taken against Edom; and his purposes, that he hath purposed against the inhabitants of Teman: Surely the least of the flock shall draw them out: surely he shall make their habitations desolate with them.
The earth is moved at the noise of their fall, at the cry the noise thereof was heard in the Red sea.
Behold, he shall come up and fly as the eagle, and spread his wings over Bozrah: and at that day shall the heart of the mighty men of Edom be as the heart of a woman in her pangs.

23.pericope_label: Concerning Damascus. Hamath is confounded, and Arpad: for they have heard evil tidings: they are fainthearted; there is sorrow on the sea; it cannot be quiet. Damascus is waxed feeble, and turneth herself to flee, and fear hath seized on her: anguish and sorrows have taken her, as a woman in travail. How is the city of praise not left, the city of my joy! Therefore her young men shall fall in her streets, and all the men of war shall be cut off in that day, saith the Lord of hosts. And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall consume the palaces of Ben–hadad.

schools.summary: Give the kingdom's rise and subjugation, hear the exclamation as scornful irony over a city that would not be found empty, and count the kings who bore the royal name.
Defend the possessive as the prophet assuming another's person, take the particle as a plain affirmative, and read the fire as pure metaphor.
Trace the city's capture and demolition, and suppose the lament is put into the mouth of the Syrian king.
Sets the kingdom north as Edom lay south and makes the ruin of the capital the ruin of the whole.

debates.question: Who speaks the lament over the city of joy?

positions.position: The prophet, assuming another's person as prophets often do, and exulting very cuttingly in doing so.
The Syrian king is supposed to be the speaker.
An exclamation half scornful and half ironical, pointing back to the failed flight, since the city would not be found empty when taken.

outliers.claim: Rejects the reading that makes the following particle assign a reason, that the city is destroyed for its long persecution of the Church, preferring the simpler sense of a plain affirmative.
Offers a literal option for the fire, that the houses built upon the wall were set alight by the Chaldeans, against Calvin's reading of it as metaphor throughout.

themes: Concerning Damascus. Hamath is confounded, and Arpad: for they have heard evil tidings: they are fainthearted; there is sorrow on the sea; it cannot be quiet.
Damascus is waxed feeble, and turneth herself to flee, and fear hath seized on her: anguish and sorrows have taken her, as a woman in travail.
How is the city of praise not left, the city of my joy!
Therefore her young men shall fall in her streets, and all the men of war shall be cut off in that day, saith the Lord of hosts.
And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall consume the palaces of Ben–hadad.

28.pericope_label: Concerning Kedar, and concerning the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon shall smite, thus saith the Lord; Arise ye, go up to Kedar, and spoil the men of the east. Their tents and their flocks shall they take away: they shall take to themselves their curtains, and all their vessels, and their camels; and they shall cry unto them, Fear is on every side. Flee, get you far off, dwell deep, O ye inhabitants of Hazor, saith the Lord; for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon hath taken counsel against you, and hath conceived a purpose against you.

schools.summary: Doubt that Hazor is a city at all and take it for a district, and hear in the cry of terror the prophet's own characteristic phrase.
Fit the tents and curtains to a shepherd people with no fields or cities, and read the counsel taken against them as capture by craft rather than strength.
Identify the plunderers and read the command to dwell deep as a retreat into the desert, while confessing the site of Hazor cannot be found.
Draws the whole manner of life into a portrait: no walls, no treasure but stock, no soldiers, no merchants, and yet rich.

positions.position: Petra itself, the metropolis whose king had petty kings under him, and certainly not the Canaanite Hazor.
The head city of several kingdoms in Joshua's time.
A people originally Canaanite, driven from the northern kingdom of that name and settled among the Kedarenes.
Probably not a city but a district, since the name belongs to many Palestinian places while the pairing with Kedar points elsewhere.
The place cannot be found: no doubt in Arabia and of consequence once, but now no more.

outliers.claim: Takes the counsel and the purpose to mean the secret means by which the king subdued a people who feared nothing, preparing and dividing his forces so that they were taken by craft rather than strength.
Describes the Kedarenes as a Bedouin nation dwelling in tents through the whole region between Arabia Petraea and Babylonia.

themes: Concerning Kedar, and concerning the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon shall smite, thus saith the Lord; Arise ye, go up to Kedar, and spoil the men of the east.
Their tents and their flocks shall they take away: they shall take to themselves their curtains, and all their vessels, and their camels; and they shall cry unto them, Fear is on every side.
Flee, get you far off, dwell deep, O ye inhabitants of Hazor, saith the Lord; for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon hath taken counsel against you, and hath conceived a purpose against you.

31.pericope_label: Arise, get you up unto the wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care, saith the Lord, which have neither gates nor bars, which dwell alone. And their camels shall be a booty, and the multitude of their cattle a spoil: and I will scatter into all winds them that are in the utmost corners; and I will bring their calamity from all sides thereof, saith the Lord. And Hazor shall be a dwelling for dragons, and a desolation for ever: there shall no man abide there, nor any son of man dwell in it.

schools.summary: Notes that the camels and cattle are named as booty because they were the whole of the plunder such a people could furnish, and renders the creatures of the desolation jackals.
Render the epithet secure rather than wealthy, insist the command to go up is the Lord's, and explain why the prophets people a deserted land with dragons.
Render the nation peaceable, ascribe the order to march to the king's own counsels, and read the utmost corners as the coasts of the peninsula.

debates.question: Who gives the command to go up against the nation at ease?

positions.position: The Lord, who commissions both the king and his forces; the words are not the king's counsel nor his address to his army.
The king, the order being the outcome of his deliberations against a people who had no neighbours able to help them.

outliers.claim: Explains why the prophets say a deserted land becomes the habitation of dragons, since that is more grievous than the land merely standing empty and so makes a deeper impression of God's judgment.

Holds the desolation absolute, that the place is never to be repeopled and may be visited occasionally but never made a permanent abode, where Gill allows the perpetuity to mean at least a very long time.

themes: Arise, get you up unto the wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care, saith the Lord, which have neither gates nor bars, which dwell alone.

And their camels shall be a booty, and the multitude of their cattle a spoil: and I will scatter into all winds them that are in the utmost corners; and I will bring their calamity from all sides thereof, saith the Lord.
And Hazor shall be a dwelling for dragons, and a desolation for ever: there shall no man abide there, nor any son of man dwell in it.

34.pericope_label: The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah the prophet against Elam in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, saying, Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might. And upon Elam will I bring the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and will scatter them toward all those winds; and there shall be no nation whither the outcasts of Elam shall not come.

schools.summary: Weigh the unique date attached to this oracle against the argument from the missing royal name, and read the four winds as a cyclone on a threshing-floor.
Deny that Elam means Persia on the ground that the Persians never injured the Jews, and generalise the bow into each nation's peculiar art of war.
Identify Elam with Persia or with the Greek Elymais, and take the four winds for armies drawn from many provinces.
Accepts the date for the whole group of oracles and draws from the broken bow that what we most trust to fails us first.

positions.position: The Persians, descended from a son of Shem.
Not Persia but the distinct country of Elymais, later absorbed into the Persian empire.
Nearer the Parthians than the Persians, since the Persians were remote from the Jews and never injured them, so no prophet had cause to denounce them.
A Semitic people in the Persian province of Susiana.

outliers.claim: Observes that this is the only oracle in these two chapters with a date attached, and reports the counter-argument that the absence of the conqueror's name points to an earlier date rather than a later one.
Uses the date to sever rather than to place the oracle, concluding it can have no natural or historical connection with the other prophecies gathered in this chapter.

themes: The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah the prophet against Elam in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, saying,
Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might.
And upon Elam will I bring the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and will scatter them toward all those winds; and there shall be no nation whither the outcasts of Elam shall not come.

37.pericope_label: For I will cause Elam to be dismayed before their enemies, and before them that seek their life: and I will bring evil upon them, even my fierce anger, saith the Lord; and I will send the sword after them, till I have consumed them: And I will set my throne in Elam, and will destroy from thence the king and the princes, saith the Lord. But it shall come to pass in the latter days, that I will bring again the captivity of Elam, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: States the principle that the Lord's throne is the throne of whichever king is for the time his chosen instrument, here the Chaldean against whom Elam had risen.
Infer from the severity that the Elamites had raged against God's people, read the throne as a tribunal, and admit that no restoration is recorded in history.
Assign the throne to Cyrus or Alexander as God's gift, and find the promised restoration fulfilled in Elamites converted at Pentecost.

debates.question: What is the throne God sets in Elam?

positions.position: The throne of the conqueror, called God's because God gave it to him.
The throne of whichever king is for the time God's chosen instrument, here the Chaldean.
Not a royal seat but a tribunal: God avenges himself as though his court were erected in that land.

debates.question: What is the restoration in the latter days?

positions.position: The times of the Messiah, since the liberty enjoyed under Cyrus was too near to be called the latter days.
Probably the spiritual freedom given under the gospel, though the union with Persia under Cyrus is also in view.
Either sense may stand: after many days, which would point to Cyrus, or the time of the Messiah, evidenced by Elamites converted at Pentecost.
No restoration of the nation is recorded in history at all; the hope is that they should be united under Christ as their head.

outliers.claim: Argues from the severity of the sentence that the Elamites must have been among the chief of God's enemies, or at least cruel in no ordinary way and delighting in slaughter.
Confesses that difficulties remain and that who the Elamites were is still a question, his best answer being that they and the Persians were two distinct peoples afterwards blended.

themes: For I will cause Elam to be dismayed before their enemies, and before them that seek their life: and I will bring evil upon them, even my fierce anger, saith the Lord; and I will send the sword after them, till I have consumed them:
And I will set my throne in Elam, and will destroy from thence the king and the princes, saith the Lord.
But it shall come to pass in the latter days, that I will bring again the captivity of Elam, saith the Lord.
